speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to move a motion of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Given that the government is about to manipulate and change the composition of the consumer price index, and given the importance placed on the consumer price index as a measure of the cost of living by governments, by business, by labour and by consumers, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom):

subsubtopic: EXTENT OF REDUCTION OF GOVERNMENT INTERVENTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to put a question to the Minister of Finance. Noting that the working paper with respect to the government's post control position concludes that there should be less direct government intervention and an increased reliance on the market economy, would the minister add credence to these words by indicating to what extent it is planned to arrest the growth of Crown corporations. For example, is it planned to abandon PetroCan's intervention in the market economy?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
subsubtopic: EXTENT OF REDUCTION OF GOVERNMENT INTERVENTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the role that Petro-Canada is already playing and can play as a catalyst in providing wider exploration in the frontier areas of Canada seems to be the very best argument for that kind of role by government. Indeed, there will be some areas where, for example, in manpower retraining, on which my colleague will have the occasion to speak, the role of the government will be reduced and that of the private sector increased. Particularly in determining the adequacy of Canada's energy resources and petroleum and natural gas resources in frontier areas, we still believe that Petro-Canada can and will play a very effective role.

subsubtopic: EXTENT OF REDUCTION OF GOVERNMENT INTERVENTION
speechtext: In view of the fact that the year old white paper entitled "Attack on Inflation" expressed the commitments "to reassess the costs to the private sector of many government rules and regulations" and to review the inflationary impact of its own regulatory agencies, and further noting that this commitment is reaffirmed in both the throne speech and the working paper tabled yesterday, would the minister point to any specific instances of deregulation or changes in regulation which will have the effect aimed for in the white paper and the subsequent references which I have noted?

subsubtopic: EXTENT OF REDUCTION OF GOVERNMENT INTERVENTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have the occasion to refer again to the actions being undertaken by my colleagues with respect to the filing requirements imposed on the private sector, particularly the small business sector, which we think will be very effective in reducing the administrative load which those companies will have to bear in dealing with the government of Canada. We hope that, in turn, we will have co-operative action from provincial governments so that the collective imposition by government of regulations on the private sector will be reduced.

subtopic: POSSIBLE INTRODUCTION OF NEGATIVE INCOME TAX
POSSIBLE INTRODUCTION OF NEGATIVE INCOME TAX
speechtext:
I have another supplementary question for the Minister of Finance. As the working paper dealing with the government's role in the post control period tabled yesterday states the following:

It will be necessary to pursue an examination of the integration of income transfers with the tax system.
Would the minister be more explicit and indicate to the House if this is a wordy way of stating that it is intended to introduce a negative income tax?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: POSSIBLE INTRODUCTION OF NEGATIVE INCOME TAX
speechtext: That is not so. I would point out to the hon. gentleman that, indeed, under the arrangements for supplementary old age security payments we already have just such a system. It will be important to the activities of my colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and others of my colleagues to pursue ways in which the tax system can be integrated with the transfer payments we now have.

subtopic: METHOD OF REVIEWING PROVISION OF GOVERNMENT SERVICES AND TRANSFERRING SOME TO PRIVATE SECTOR
METHOD OF REVIEWING PROVISION OF GOVERNMENT SERVICES AND TRANSFERRING SOME TO PRIVATE SECTOR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the President of the Treasury Board. Having regard to the gestures which the government has advanced, both in the Speech from the Throne and in the documents tabled yesterday, aimed at expanding the role of the private sector and having regard to the proposition that all federal government programs will be under review, can the minister advise the House just precisely what form that review will take, what criteria the review will be based upon and who will be conducting it? Would he also elaborate and tell the House what initiatives the government is planning to permit the private sector to provide those goods and services which were referred to in the document yesterday which are now being handled by government sources or agencies?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (President of the Treasury Board):
subtopic: METHOD OF REVIEWING PROVISION OF GOVERNMENT SERVICES AND TRANSFERRING SOME TO PRIVATE SECTOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think any elaboration I make today would follow on the comments of my colleague, the Minister of Finance. With regard to those services which are clearly public and the government responsibility, we are looking at our expenditures very carefully. Indeed, we have been doing that for some time now, and that is a process which 1 intend to continue.
With regard to those services which are being provided by Crown corporations, I do not think I can make any further comments beyond those my colleague the Minister of Finance made, except to say that the matter is under very serious review to determine what might be better provided by the private sector, but certainly with the proviso that those goods and services must continue to be made available effectively to the public whether through the private sector or through public intervention.

subtopic: METHOD OF REVIEWING PROVISION OF GOVERNMENT SERVICES AND TRANSFERRING SOME TO PRIVATE SECTOR
speechtext:

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne spoke abundantly of national unity. Paradoxically, in his reply to the House, the Prime Minister (Mr.Trudeau) did not breathe a word of it.
I refuse to believe, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister chose deliberately to ignore the prime concern of all Canadians. In all indulgence, I attribute the behaviour of the leader of the government to the shock he must have suffered when his Minister of National Defence resigned for strange and enigmatic reasons. It therefore behoves us of the official opposition to make up for the pusillanimity of the Prime Minister in the House and broach openly this delicate matter which some would sweep under the rug.
To remain silent at this time would justly provoke the anger of my fellow citizens. To remain silent while federal institutions are cracking up in various places would amount to ratifying national suicide. People are well aware, Mr. Speaker, of the reaction against the implementation of the Official Languages Act, they are aware of the inequity suffered by many citizens for various reasons, and they are well aware that in the province of Quebec, resignation has given way to impatience to such a point that I feel in the majority of Quebecers, since 1973, a disgust which could soon be expressed in the provincial election by a spectacular increase in the popular vote for the independence movement and which could realistically give at least 30 seats to the Parti Quebecois.
In this morning's Devoir, Mr. Michel Roy, with his usual insight, asked this question, and I quote:
Does Canada want to separate from Quebec?
[Mr. Chretien.)
His intellectual integrity should have made Mr. Roy ask the real question, which is: Does Canada want to separate from the Liberal Party? We already know what would be the reply of the Canadian people. If the Liberals in Quebec are defeated in the next elections, I shall not be heartbroken, and I know that several of my friends opposite share this feeling. Moreover, the fact that a wish for change should be felt at all levels of society does not surprise me either; and if a new team should replace an inadequate team bogged down in mediocrity, this would not worry me in the least. What frightens me is that this feeling which is getting stronger and stronger in one of the two Canadian majorities has increased as the federal government has demonstrated inability, delays, contradictions and arrogance. And on this last point, neither the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Joyal) nor the Gens de Pair will disagree with me.

Mr. Speaker, on this issue of national unity, this speech from the throne is an indication of just how sad and muddled the present government is in its approach to the challenge.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
When the problem is people, they put their faith in a piece of paper. When the questions are complex, they hide behind the simplistic and the shallow. Let me be precise.
The question of the constitution is quite separate from the question of national unity. Only the most partisan of interests would suggest the blurring of both concerns-blurring, by the way, which could seriously make national unity the victim of a badly thought-out approach. The people of Canada want their constitution brought home. We want the right to be able to change the rules of the game in our own way as a mature and sovereign nation. We can benefit measurably from the final instrument of independence. That instrument, however, is not the panacea that the government opposite hopes it will be. It is, more realistically, a test-a test of the maturity of our nation, a test which we will have to respond to by both bringing it home and making it work for Canadians. It is a document which has not served this nation badly over the years, a document that can serve all Canadians more effectively at home.
I ask this government to be cognizant of one thing. The bringing home of a constitution is, in the thrust of things, a symbolic gesture symbolizing maturity, independence, consensus and unity. If it is done in such a way so as to threaten the very qualities the constitution seeks to symbolize, then the onus for that will be on the heads of this government and its leader.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) might indeed like to see the members of our party oppose the return of the constitution so that he might fan this issue as only he knows how. But that will not happen. We are at peace with the patriation of the constitution. We embrace its importance and its significance. We understand what was to be the Victoria charter. We
October 15, 1976

understand what the premiers have said to each other and what they have said to Ottawa, and we are impressed with the room for moderation and understanding on all sides. We obviously have more faith than some opposite. He believed, and I believe, as well as responsible English and French speaking Canadians believe, that the two principles are still synonymous. A parliament approves a principle; a government makes that principle operate fairly. This government has failed. It cannot make the principle work fairly because Canadians do not believe that if is fair or that it can be fair. All the deathbed conversions in the world will change nothing. The damage is too great. The wounds are too deep.
This country deserves a government that will make bilingualism and fairness synonymous, that will make equality of opportunity synonymous with encouragement, not with discrimination; that will make second language skill a factor of opportunity and not simply one of compulsion and threat.

Mr. Speaker, if the Prime Minister had not strived to systematically undermine our constitutional regime and to stealthily assume responsibilities which de jure fall under provincial jurisdiction; had he not, on so many occasions and against so many people, used abusive language; had he not given such hopes to so many Canadians whom he deceived eventually miserably; had he not been, regarding controls, so shamelessly deceitful towards the people, he would not have created around him such an hostile climate which now compromises even his most commendable initiatives.
However, the Prime Minister seems ill-advised to maintain that even general bilingualism in the public service of Canada constitutes almost the only condition of Canada's survival as a political entity.
Bilingualism is undoubtedly important for the future unity of Confederation. But this country's unity also requires the federal government to uphold a general policy that is acceptable to everybody. We will be in a better position to achieve such unity in this country when the government stops treating the provinces as competitors rather than associates and when it sincerely asks them to take part in the development of national policies. We will achieve this goal more quickly when this government further promotes the development of regional communities according to their own dynamism.
The main feature of Canadian federalism must be the free development of these communities within the framework of national goals which are not too demanding. But in this regard the government deserves some blame. If its bilingualism policy was not welcome in many circles, it is not only because of its deficiencies and the wrong directions it takes but also because the government is vigorously opposed to many legitimate regional expectations.
The day Ottawa will stop acting like a steamroller, the day they will stop trying to hoard for their sole benefit all the live forces of the country, that day we will no longer have to worry seriously about the future of the Canadian Confederation.

What are the chances of a peaceful solution, and what role, if any, could Canada be called upon to play in this area? Or do we leave it to Dr. Kissinger to tell us what we should do and how much we should pay? What exactly will be Canada's role in formulating the new economic order? Many Canadians who came from eastern Europe still experience difficulties in reaching families and members of their families there or obtaining authorization to bring their relatives into Canada. Without commenting on the role played by the U.S.S.R., I would certainly like to see more frequent discussions of the problem of family reunification in order to improve upon what we can term a still uneasy friendship. I,

myself, am looking forward to the opportunity of becoming better acquainted with the problems in east-west relations.
We all witness with anguish the arms build-up in eastern Europe, in the Middle East and elsewhere, with the risk of new military clashes between neighbouring states. We are not yet immune from a nuclear catastrophe, and we want to know what Canada is doing to help accelerate detente and nuclear disarmament. With regard to selling our nuclear technology to developing countries, we are still a long way from a satisfactory level of safeguards and a really effective system of international inspection.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs spoke the other day in reassuring terms of our dedication to the survival of Israel as an independent state, while remaining friendly toward the Arab world. I agree with him; but we would like to know more about his veiled threat of withdrawing from the United Nations peacekeeping operations in Cyprus and possibly elsewhere. Is saving money the main consideration now for this government? Are we going to abandon the traditional policy which endeared Canada to the whole world particularly relating to peacekeeping? Has the government given any consideration to the German and Israeli proposals dealing with terrorism?
As far as our relations with the United States are concerned, they certainly need to be improved. This government remains seemingly undisturbed, as if irritants were normal between friends. It is high time we did our utmost to try to solve outstanding issues before they get worse.

To that end more is needed than chance encounters between ministers or heads of governments. We must entertain a constant flow of communications with the American Congress and administration and keep the American people better informed of our views.
Canada is about to become again a member of the Security Council, and as such we are going to be called upon almost daily to express our opinions on current problems and to cast important and perhaps decisive votes. So I do not think the problem of French is only in the air. I do not know what would happen with English-speaking westerners if they had to wonder if they have the right to speak English at home. The problem is crucial. I want this country to remain united as much as the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe.
Those are, Mr. Speaker, principles and things that can be advocated in a very serene and very positive way. From which side of the House did the protests come? The outcry of indignation came from those (wo Liberal members, because in our party, there is no resignation, there is no giving up, there is no quitting because we disagree; there is room for struggle within our party and this is what the hon. members for Maisonneuve-Rosemont and Matane are doing. I will speak about that later. I also want to criticize the government but I
October 15, 1976

will try to be positive, contrarily to the members of the official opposition to whom I have been listening these last days. Their speeches are negative. After this short digression, I will now speak about a program in which I and the people from my riding are greatly interested, namely the Local Initiatives Program.
1 also had to fight within the department. The Department of Manpower is responsible for LIP and I never saw so many people disagreeing with a program. I take my riding as an example, and I could as well take many others such as Beauce or Lotbiniere. I have never seen such a disagreement. My riding submitted 53 requests amounting to $1,400,000 and got a budget of $195,000 or 14 per cent of the requests.
Even if I were to accept 8 or 10 projects, I would deceive a lot of people. Never before has a program disappointed so many people. The publicity urged people to submit ideas. Maybe the leader of the opposition is the only one who has no ideas. People were told: If you have ideas tell them to the manpower centre; if you are creative, come to the manpower centre. People were often invited through a publicity that I consider perhaps not misleading but at least abusive. When you whet appetites, you have to satisfy them. The government must find the moneys required and, if it does not have them, then I agree that it should do away with LIP and implement a program to create jobs, not for 30 weeks, but on a permanent basis.
I know that, in the Speech from the Throne, and I am very happy about it, there are recommendations to that effect. The minister will make recommendations with a view to creating jobs, to promote creativity, and that means creating permanent employment. With the Opportunities for Youth program, we had exactly the same problem. If the riding of Levis is granted 10 projects, on the assumption that, in the summer, four to ten students will work for each one of them, we will quit going over the same ground all the time. In fact, this is a race. I was visited by those who work on those projects, a delegation of 53 persons; I had 53 telephone calls from malcontents. Not that I am afraid of that but when one has whetted appetites, one has to see to it that they are satisfied.
I shall now speak of another recommendation. I spoke of integrating the students in community projects. I have been struggling for a long time now to obtain that those students who want to work in industry can do so. I myself lived through that experience. I have asked the unions several times to include in their collective agreements a stipulation whereby, even though a student is not a member of the union, the company is authorized to hire him. A given industry could hire a dozen students during the summer time and so enable them to pay for their studies.
Many other topics could be dealt with. One of them will interest several of my fellow-citizens of the province of Quebec, specially in the agricultural ridings. As a member for a Quebec riding, I am particularly concerned about the absence, in the Speech from the Throne, of any mention of the reforms to be brought in the field of agriculture, and the dairy policy. In Quebec, milk producers will be faced with bankrupt-

cy in the near future unless the present policy is changed. On the one hand, the producers are penalized for exceeding their quotas; on the other hand, and I am very well informed about this matter, the producers are short of milk if they want to achieve full capacity. That is the ridiculous contradiction the present system produces. We have lost face enough before our fellow-citizens. I hope the government will have understood this. I dare hope that the Cabinet will put forward the proposals formulated by the Quebec caucus which had been supported by the caucus of the other provinces, particularly for the increase in milk quotas, which would partly solve the problem of the penalties imposed on surpluses for those who have been unjustly and unfairly treated.
Mr. Speaker, there is another subject alluded to in the Speech from the Throne: unemployment insurance. As I said to the Progressive Conservative hon. member who was here earlier, I do not want to make a negative speech. As far as the Unemployment Insurance Act is concerned, it is really extraordinary to note the number of cases we have to pass on to our secretaries in riding offices for solution. I know that we are about to amend the act. For the average man, this act is not really clear. It is incomprehensible.
The government should provide people with a summary of the rights and obligations of beneficiaries, that whenever there is a dismissal, a lay off or a termination of employment the employer be compelled to hand a certificate which would have to be produced. I have witnessed very pitiful cases during summer and in more than a year. People are not informed and I think we will have to do something. Indeed it would be a very practical solution. When an employee is fired, the employer hands him his unemployment insurance book with a summary of this law to inform him clearly of his right and obligations.
I felt therefore I had to make such a recommendation to the government and I hope it will act on it in the near future. In any case, whenever the Unemployment Insurance Act comes up for discussion and amendment I shall participate in the debate in a very positive way and make recommendations to the government.
I will now turn to another subject and I will be very short, Mr. Speaker. 1 hope this will be the last time I rise on the issue. In the nearly fourteen years that I have been sitting in this place, I remember having fought battles along with the hon. member for Langelier (Mr. Marchand) even before he was elected to this House. I led a battle about coastal shipping and the merchant marine.
I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that people have been preparing reports, making studies and asking questions for quite some time. I, for one, gave notice of a motion to urge the government to implement the recommendations of the Darling Report on the merchant marine. And I know very well that in a very near future a common front-a formula dear to unions-will gather across Canada to revive the debate on the merchant marine issue.

October 15, 1976
The Address-Mr. R. Guay
I request the government to appoint somebody for the examination of all those things. I know that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) has already dealt with those issues. I know that the Department of Industry is considering their consequences. I know that the Department of Finance is involved. In fact, it seems to me that no one is responsible. That is what I ask with much insistance. I hope it is for the last time. If we do not want a merchant marine, I want the government to say so to the Canadian people and we will forget about it, period. Let no one tell us there will be further studies will be made. No. And if the government does not know the Darling Report recommendations, I could repeat them.
In an industrial country like Canada, with the longest rivers in the world, we have no merchant marine. We own no ship. We are an exporting country and we have no merchant marine.
Lately I got many telegrams from various shipyards. We no longer have the policy we used to have. The STAP program gave assistance for building ships ordered by foreign countries. Subsidies amount to approximately 17 per cent whereas they previously reached 40 per cent. This program was discontinued. What is the future of our shipyards? In my area, a shipyard has already closed. I remember quite well when it happened because it was during an electoral campaign: 1,000 people were suddenly out of work. Does this government plan to do the same thing with other shipyards? And mine is not the only area where this problem can surface. It is going to affect every shipyard all over the country. And we know for a fact that over 12,000 people-I say 12,000-in Quebec and Ontario alone I think are employed in shipbuilding.
So, Mr. Speaker, the cabinet will have to be more united, better coordinated if the responsibility is to be entrusted to someone who, in accordance with the recommendations of the Darling report, will recommend to us, Canadians, that we have our own merchant marine. The recommendations of the Darling report on coastal shipping were implemented. I remember it quite well. In a year or two, the matter will be closed. Coastal shipping and a merchant marine were always at issue.
We made our point. And I am convinced that the government will listen and take my remarks into consideration. Let them read the report once again and abstain from asking for still another report and further studies. That is what I said at a recent union meeting of shipyard workers. Do not submit to me any more reports to convince me that we need a merchant marine in Canada, because I am convinced. And that is the question I put to the government. I am convinced that a decision must be made. If it looks fully into all the recommendations of the Darling report, the government will have no choice but to set up a body, a Ministry of State, or to appoint a minister to implement the recommendations. We are not asking for an affirmative answer today or that two, three, four, five, six or ten billion dollars be appropriated overnight, but that a schedule be drawn up so that we may know where we stand. That is the question I put to the government because not only is it vital to the survival of shipyards and shipbuilding

in Canada but it is also vital for a country as industrialized as ours, as I said earlier, an exporting country, to have a merchant marine when other small countries have their own. Our prestige would be enhanced on the international level.
The Liberal government was able to understand the needs of our economy in the past, with regard to coastal shipping for instance, and when it created the Department of Regional Economic Expansion in 1968. I want to commend the government because the riding of Levis and the Quebec City area are among those in Canada which have benefited the most from those job-creating grants. The minister will speak about job creating, but I think of that assistance program designed to extend update businesses or set up new ones, and I only regret that not enough funds are provided.
I know that the farmers are going to protest. I already mentioned that but only with regard to the dairy policy. Dairy farmers get $631 or $632 million from the government in the form of loans and grants, which represents close to one quarter billion dollars. However, the DREE estimates barely amount to $500 million.
Therefore, I am convinced that the present minister is doing an exceptional job. He has visited every province. Some industries should not be refused assistance for lack of funds. This is what happens in the case of LIP projects. It happened for the student assistance programs. So, let the programs be publicized, but if needs are to be created, those needs should be met.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Before beginning the speech I wish to make this afternoon, I should like to congratulate you, Mr. Deputy Speaker, on your reappointment this session and to express my congratulations, also, to the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Ethier) who has joined you and who yesterday for the first time took his place in the chair presiding over the deliberations of this chamber. I can speak for my colleagues in this party and, I am sure, for members of all parties in this House when I say that the appointments to which I have referred are richly deserved and we look forward to working with you as this session continues.
I should also like to say here in the chamber what I have said directly to the mover and seconder of the address in reply, the hon. member for Restigouche (Mr. Harquail) and the hon. member for Lafontaine-Rosemont (Mr. Lachance), that is, to offer them my congratulations for the honour accorded to them and on the manner in which they delivered their
October 15, 1976

speeches. Although those hon. members sit on the other side of the House and we have our disagreements from time to time, I am glad to say that their families who were here to watch from the gallery on that occasion, as well as their constituents who will no doubt read the speeches when they are distributed, have reason to be proud of the way in which this responsibility was discharged.
I should like, also, to join my leader in paying tribute to the Governor General of Canada and his lady. Anyone who has watched the struggle of a loved one to recover from the devastation of a stroke, as I did in the case of my own mother, cannot fail to be moved by that man's persistence and courage in the face of adversity. I think, too, of the support and encouragement which Madam Leger is giving her husband on every occasion, particularly on this occasion, the most public of all, the opening of parliament.
The past months have been eventful months indeed, particularly the months since October 12, 1975, when the Liberal government embraced the controls they had damned in the course of the election campaign. Those months have been a devastating experience for the government-perhaps in the minds of many people that is not too unfortunate-but they have also been a devastating experience for the public generally. In support of this statement 1 am not relying on public opinion polls, although one cannot completely discount them.
Nor do I rely on the opinions of columnists who hon. gentlemen opposite may judge to be unfriendly toward them. Rather, I rely on what I see before my eyes-a government which is lurching from crisis to crisis, important ministers leaving, or being left to occupy either of the extreme ends of the front benches, the space which has been described as the St. Helena or the Elba of the Privy Council. I shall not easily forget the look on the faces of the supporters of the government when they were justifiably flayed by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) on Wednesday.
What has happened to this administration, Mr. Speaker, is that it has played the power game, and played it for the sake of the game rather than using the rules of the game for the purpose for which the game was created, and that is to govern and lead. It was not always so with this government, but it has become abundantly clear now that that is the level to which it has fallen.
I would not want you to think that the government does not have its apologists. It does have them in abundance, but within the once great Liberal party there are thoughtful people at the grass roots in a constituency like Ottawa-Carleton or St. John's West who are standing back and are shocked by what has happened to the party which brought forth the likes of Laurier and St. Laurent, the latter whom we honoured this morning. They are turning away from the party in despair, and in droves. These apologists grasp at straws to justify this fall from grace. They will tell you that this Gethsemane through which they are passing is some form of martyrdom, when it is really the result of a failure of vision and loss of a sense of
The Address-Mr. W. Baker
purpose and a sense of vitality that a sense of purpose can bring to any government.
I am, quite frankly, alarmed as a Canadian that some of these apologists would adopt the simplistic approach that the only reason for unpopularity is that the country is against bilingualism and the Anti-Inflation Board. To say that in respect of bilingualism is to say that the majority of Canadians are prepared to deny the sense of equity, fairness and justice that is, and was, the purpose of the Official Languages Act. That position, if that is the position of the government which has been expressed by some of its apologists, most notably and recently by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), is hypocritical at very best.
That is not to say that Canadians are not upset by the way the government has chosen to implement the principle in some areas. The public service of Canada has felt the sting of its stupidity, the double-talk, changing statistics, the force-feeding, the overzealous designation of positions, all of which has taken place because the government has been out of touch with reality for a long period of time. They ignored the warnings of their friends, and even the man I defeated was one of those. They ignored the warnings of Keith Spicer, a servant of this House, and they paid half a million dollars to Professor Bibeau to be told that which every public servant knew, that the program, though well-intentioned, was misdirected; and when the chips are down, and that is their equivalent to the Gallup poll statistics, they suddenly flip-flop.
Look at the words in the Speech from the Throne. The government would leave the impression with us, from those words, that it intends to treat the public service with the benign neglect that Mr. Spicer suggested. The throne speech implies that the pace of implementation will slacken-and I use the world "implies" advisedly-while just a few days earlier, in that true confession session in a hotel in Toronto, the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) said it could not slacken. I quote from the Ottawa Citizen of October 4, which states:
Mr. Roberts also says a slowdown in the rate at which bilingualism is being implemented in the public service would be a severe blow to national unity.
More double-talk. I have spoken many times in the House and outside about this matter. I represent a large number of public servants. There are certainly other problems in the public service, and I have spoken about them as well.
It is a fact that morale is low in our public service. It should be high, but it is not. The great majority of literally thousands of letters and telephone calls I have received and discussions that I have had with public servants tell me that the public service has accepted the principle of the Official Languages Act which, put simply, is that an English-speaking Canadian in Hamilton and a French-speaking Canadian in Chicoutimi have the right to address and be addressed in one or other of the official languages by their government. The public servant does not need Professor Bibeau to inform him or her that the scope and extent of designation is out of proportion to the need, that the language teaching system is unsound, that the usefulness of training on the job was at best overrated, and

October 15, 1976
The Address-Mr. W. Baker
that the cost in dollar terms and in human terms demands some change.
1 do not know how many times a government has to be told this, but surely no reasonable person would suggest that to question doubtful implementation procedures is equivalent to a denial of the principle. Here we have the case of the throne speech saying one thing and a minister of the Crown saying another. Is it any wonder there is skepticism? Is it any wonder that anyone who has witnessed the performance of this government in the sensitive area of implementation in the public service could be anything but at least skeptical?
If, as we expected, in the course of the debate there is an enlargement of the so-called assurances in the Speech from the Throne, the public service will not accept them now. That is the position we have come to. They accept them for what they are, and that is words, sir-mere words. That is why the commitment to examine the concerns about implementation given by the Leader of the Opposition the other day is so important in the national capital and in the nation itself.
The plain truth of the matter is that if there is any relationship in the field of language to the problem of national unity, and I think there is some, the problems began not with the passage of the statute, in my judgment, but with the methods used by the government to implement the principle. If there is to be any lessening of the difficulties in terms of national unity-and I respectfully suggest that any government worth its salt would re-examine its position in terms of implementation-well, we will see what this government says but, more important, we will want to see what this government does.
I read on in the speech and noticed that the government had been smitten with a sudden revelation that the place to learn a second language was first in the schools with the young people, rather than those who have advanced to the middle and later years. The government did not need Professor Bibeau to tell it that. It did not need Keith Spicer, either, to tell it that. The parents in the national capital area and the parents in this country as a whole could have told the government that just as well. Even the government's opponents were telling it that.
What has been the government's commitment in the past to this important part of the bilingual policy? To be sure, money is being spent on language training in the schools, but it is pitifully small in terms of the magnitude of the problem. However, it is being spent. But can this government be trusted here? I do not know, and I am sure there is some skepticism among the four boards of education in the national capital area based on the performance of this government. No sooner did it have the boards committed to a very important experimental training program, the results of which would have been in use all over this country-and that was the intention-those boards, having based their commitment on a commitment of funds from the federal government, the federal government denied the boards a source of funds.
This has had a profound effect on language training in the national capital, on the people in that program and on the
[Mr. Baker (Grenville-Carleton).l
future of language training. If past performance is any guide to us, then it is a shaky foundation upon which to build any faith in this government, even in that area. Again we will have to wait for the performance.
Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) spoke in Toronto of national unity. The real blow to national unity has been this government's attitude that it was always right when events have shown that it is almost always wrong. It assumed that bilingualism was the only vehicle for national unity. Certainly it is an important one, but not to the exclusion of other considerations. The leader of our party mentioned the problem of regional disparity respecting unity. The whole transportation problem facing Canada will affect national unity. Lack of an energy policy will have an effect on national unity. The ease with which the federal government backs out of cost-sharing programs, without so much as a fare thee well, affects national unity. The medicare scheme is a good example of that.
The surprises in the federal taxation, imposed without consultation, on resources in this country have an effect on national unity. The failure of this government to tackle disparity in terms of decentralizing productive industrial capacity will affect national unity. Language is not the only factor in national unity, but because of the preoccupation of this government with language, its tunnel-vision approach to the question of national unity, and our feelings about ourselves it has suffered considerably at its hands.
The other excuse upon which the apologists for this administration rely to explain their fall from grace is the suggestion that Canadians are against the war on inflation. Mr. Speaker, that is as simplistic as it is untrue. Canadians are not against the war on inflation. They are against the deceit-and they were deceived by a government that said one thing when it asked for a mandate and acted in another way when the country gave it that mandate. Canadians have no time for such a fraudulent performance. This is what they are really telling the government by virtue of the opinion polls and by any other indicator which one would like to use. Even the defectors from the government, and there have been a number, are telling them the same thing.
Mr. Speaker, if this government had any political character to begin with, it has now lost it and that character has been replaced by political expendiency and a litany of failure. The most obvious failure, of course, is to stem the stampede of ministers out of the ranks. Or one could choose this government's attitude to scandal, the sheer cosmetic quality of its approaches to the problems facing Canada. I make no comments on the reasons for the resignation of the Minister of National Defence except to say that his constitutional theories, at least as they relate to numbers, are questionable. But his leaving, the time he chose to leave and the circumstances under which he made this announcement, are significant. While his action may be judged by some as premature or for the wrong reasons, the act of leaving is itself an indication of the extent of the rot in this government.
October 15, 1976

Mr. Speaker, 1 spoke a few moments ago about national unity, the importance of it to our country and the importance of it, as well, to our capacity to tackle the things that must be tackled if the legitimate aspirations of the people of Canada are to be met. It is a fact, I think-I believe I can state this safely-that even a government dedicated to disunity could not have done a better job than this government. For some reason or other the present administration has forgotten how our country came about.
It was not forged in revolution, like the United States. It did not cast off any bonds at the beginning. It came together by agreement, or at least by consensus and understanding, because there were some reluctant participants at the outset, as you know, Mr. Speaker.
Since there was consensus in 1867 and before that, a good case was made for creating a nation in the northern half of North America. The fact that it came together by agreement and consultation, compromise and understanding, has made our confederation a very delicate thing indeed. Mr. Speaker, our confederation will continue to exist only so long as those elements of compromise, understanding, agreement and consensus exist in the minds of those who have authority in the various jurisdictions of our country. Even if we would wish it otherwise, the geography of the country, the relative isolation and population in Canada, the fact it is stretched across a rather thin line in terms of the vastness of the land, made a federal state relevant to the Fathers of Confederation, and that relevance continues today.
Federalism, as we know it in Canada, as it was conceived at the outset, is not to be subjected to confrontation, and yet that has been the principle weapon of this government in dealing with the provinces. And much of the distrust of the federal government springs from the use of that element as a tool in federal-provincial relations. I view a federal state as one in which it is possible for a strong central government to work in concert with strong provincial governments. But somehow or other the equation of confederation has gone out of balance. The atmosphere has been poisoned by the emotionalism of the threat of unilateral patriation.
I do not foresee the situation developing very quickly where the provinces will agree on the terms and conditions for amendment of the constitution, the British North America Act. But that is no reason these discussions ought not to go on. It is obvious from all reports that there has been some progress, but I am concerned about the fears expressed by Senator Forsey that unilateral patriation, without an amending formula, will put us in a constitutional straitjacket which could make it difficult for us to meet changing problems in a world where the velocity of change is almost overwhelming.
It goes without saying, as the hon. member for Saint-Hya-cinthe (Mr. Wager) said this morning, that this party does not fear the homecoming of the constitution, if one could call it that; far from it. But the government seems intent on moving ahead with or without the consent of the provinces. I would rather the government cooled it. The atmosphere is not right and I have some doubts about this government's ability to
The Address-Mr. W. Baker
change, and the feeling is growing in Canada that there will be no change until the government itself is changed.
There is nothing about our confederation that would not make it subject to the change in attitude that was suggested by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). Perhaps it is time there was a government in Canada that would not begin its approaches to the question of federal-provincial relations from the premise that the necessary condition of negotiation is conflict. There will be differences of opinion, to be sure, but conflict and mistrust can so poison the atmosphere of negotiation that meaningful negotiations are impossible to undertake.
Mr. Speaker, it is more than merely notable that the man who came to Ottawa to save us from ourselves in 1968, as he says from time to time, has presided over the period of the greatest unrest and conflict in our history. His preoccupation with one policy, language, as the cement of confederation, to the neglect of all other considerations, has turned that cement into a wedge which is endangering our feelings toward one another. I regret that state of affairs in terms of the life of my country.
Mr. Speaker, there is one last thing I want to say. It is this same government that has proven itself so untrustworthy in so many ways that will shortly ask the House to amend its rules and Standing Orders so as to make members the handmaiden of the government; to make this a place for the expedition of government business to the exclusion of its real purpose, that of a forum for the discussion of public affairs.

speechtext:
I share the concern of the hon. member, but I wish he would let me finish my speech; then perhaps we can give him unanimous consent to make a contribution of his own.
The Speech from the Throne spoke of broadcasting the proceedings of parliament and other changes in this place. There is a much more fundamental need, that is, a change in the attitude of this government to the right of Canadians to know. The throne speech made no commitment for a freedom of information act. In fact, it contains an evasion. If the speech indicates anything at all, it is that this obsession with secrecy will continue while a study is pursued. I could approach the possibility of rule changes with much more equanimity if I knew that this government was committed to the concept of a freedom of information act in the terms that the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) has worked so diligently and so well to achieve.
Charles Lynch has said-I do not often quote Charles Lynch, but I will now; sometimes he is right, and he was right

October 15, 1976
The Address-Mr. McRae
yesterday in his column-that this government is the most secretive in the western world. I believe he is correct. The Rudnicki case-the case of a public servant wronged by his employer-contains an indication of how far this government is prepared to go in terms of secrecy.
The former minister of labour, the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. O'Connell), spoke of the necessity for instituting the machinery to examine on a long-term basis the estimates of government, not only in terms of future programs but in terms of the achievement of past programs. I suggest that that concept, without a freedom of information act, would be almost meaningless. When I look back to 1968, this same government under this Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), came before the people and exhibited a sense of purpose and fairness and held out to the Canadian people a promise of equity, justice, compassion and concern. Today, as I look across the floor, I see that not only has this government become a shambling collection of the once great, at least in the minds of some, but it has debased its mandate. Whatever the result of the confidence vote in this chamber may be, the government, does not have the confidence and trust of the Canadian people.

speakeroldname: Mr. Paul E. McRae (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have heard many speeches in the House about the difficulties of this government and the way we face these problems, but very few clear statements on where we should go and what we should do. I feel there is a lack of understanding of the complexities of the times. It is all very well to say that the government should increase or decrease the money supply, or play around with fiscal arrangements, and with simple answers can straighten out all kinds of problems. These things do not work today because these times are not the kind of times we had in the 1960s, and I am waiting for some concrete suggestions from the opposition as to how to deal with today's problems.
I suspect that the opposition is not really cognizant of the kinds of problems that are faced by governments throughout the world today. These are not ordinary times; they are unique times. Let me give two examples of the uniqueness of these times. We have never had the kind of inflation we have today, which is worldwide, and at the same time high unemployment. These things, in classic economic terms do not go together, yet they exist throughout the world and in this country at present, and as a matter of fact we are doing a good deal better than most countries to resolve these conflicting problems. I am sure that most of us grew up with the myth that there are unlimited resources and all we have to do is to get those resources developed. But all of a sudden we have a totally new concept which has come into play in the last four or five years, namely, that there is a limit to our resources, that there are severe limits to our energy resources, for example.

So these are unique times, and we have to think in terms of the problems, not just carping. Let me deal for a moment with inflation. As I said, we have had this type of inflation at least since the early 1970s and it is quite unique. It is global in its implications. It is a fact that certainly all the OECD countries and the western and industrialized countries, as well as the third and fourth worlds, are affected by this inflation. It is something with which we have to come to grips.
We have been accused of deceiving the public in the 1974 election. We did not buy the kind of program that the Tories were peddling, namely a 90-day total freeze. But at the end of the 90 days I suppose the world was going to come to an end because there were no suggestions as to where to go after that. We said there was a contingency. Let us analyse the year 1974. I believe the government has been at fault in one respect, in that we had not gone to the public to justify fully why in 1974 we did not do something which we did in 1975. I think there is a good justification for this.
Let us look at the situation in 1974. We had a period of prolonged demand inflation, inflation caused by a shortage of goods both nationally and globally. It was the kind of period which would be worsened by controls, and these are what the U.S. government applied in 1972. This created unbelievable problems, because the problem was not cost, it was demand. In mid-1974 this started to change. I might say one other thing about the time before mid-1974. Wages were not a major factor in inflation at that time; wages were lagging behind. Between the summer of 1974 and the late summer of 1975 wages began to be a factor in inflation. Costs became a factor in inflation more than before, especially costs within Canada. In the first half of 1975 wage settlements were running at an average of slightly less than 22 per cent, 21.8 per cent to be exact. Beginning to escalate into the inflationary situation was a severe cost-push problem.
That is a very different kind of inflation from the type we had in early 1974, and I think it is important that people begin to realize that. What would the Tories have done in 1974? They would have had a three months freeze, and then presumably everything would have gone away. Of course, it would not have gone away because this is a worldwide problem which has to be handled in conjunction with a whole series of other problems.
Let me talk a little about what we tried to do before we brought in controls, because this government, with the previous finance minister, made a serious effort to bring about voluntary compliance of the trade union movement and the industrial leaders of this country, but they were not successful. In September of 1975 we were faced with a whole series of wage demands which were beginning to become ridiculous, such as 71 per cent in the Post Office and over 40 per cent for Quebec teachers to catch up with the Ontario teachers who were asking for another 40 per cent. There were demands of 50 per cent, 60 per cent and 70 per cent, and these were the things we were facing.
October 15, 1976

What is a government to do? Economists throughout the country were saying that we must have some kind of control period, and so we did. What is the nature of that control period? First, we decided basically not to control prices because that is a very, very difficult thing to do over a long period, and we certainly were not going into a short control period. In my opinion, that would have created only trouble. It would have created a tight scene and then we would have had the kind of distortions which took place in the United States after 1972.
So we decided there had to be a way to control prices indirectly; without that, having an army of people administering the controls, walking into major stores and seeing how many items would have to be controlled, would not work. We assumed that this is a free enterprise system, that there was a market and that where there was good competition there should not be much problem. What did we try to do? We tried to control the two things which are factors in terms of cost. One of them is wages and the other is profits. The Tories say we should not control profits and the members of the NDP say we should not control wages, but nobody tells us what we should do. Nobody makes any suggestions except to say that we should not do this or that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
What has happened? I mentioned that in the first half of 1975 the average wage settlement was in the area of 22 per cent, or 21.8 per cent. The second quarter of 1976, which is the last quarter for which we have figures, shows wage increases of around 12 per cent. There is a decrease, there is no question about that. Since controls, profits also have decreased on the average by about 7 per cent to 8 per cent, so those two things have been controlled.
What about prices? Prices have gone, from an average increase in the year before controls of something like 11 per cent, to an average increase of something like 6.5 per cent. Hon. members immediately say that that is because of food and that food is not controlled. It certainly is controlled. It is not controlled at the farm gate, but if 60 per cent of the cost is after the farm gate-and I hear hon. members using these figures-and goes to the producer, the distributor, the packager, the advertiser, and so on, these are certainly costs; and taking food and everything else into consideration we are now down to 6.5 per cent.
While wage increases are now at 11 per cent and 12 per cent, inflation-that is, the cost of living-has come down to 6.5 per cent, and that is basically the total cost of living. So there has been a successful period. Allowing for inflation and for some extra productivity, basically speaking the workingman today is better off than he was a year ago, and the person on a fixed income, such as the senior citizen, is considerably better off than he would have been had we not gone into controls. So I do not understand why the country is so upset.
The Address-Mr. McRae
It seems to me that the control period has worked. But that is not the only thing we have to talk about, because inflation is not the only economic problem facing this country. We have the problem of high unemployment, and this is something we have not solved. We are doing much better in the inflation field than we are in the employment field, but even so this nation has created more jobs per capita than any other country among the OECD countries. Between 1971 and the third quarter of 1975 we produced something over 19 per cent new jobs, so for every four people who were working in 1971 there are now five working in Canada.
The United States only produced 8 per cent more jobs, and that is one of the best figures. Our labour force has grown at a tremendous rate, partially because of the post-war baby boom and partially because of the fact that the number of women in the labour force has grown substantially. I have a figure here with regard to the proportion of women in the labour force between the ages of 25 and 44. In 1953 the figure was 23 per cent and in 1974 it was 47 per cent.
We have too much unemployment in this country, and in the next year we have to do a great deal more in terms of creating jobs both in the private sector and, I believe, in the public sector, because I do not think we will create jobs in the private sector at the rate we need to create them. We will have to do something about our 7 per cent unemployment rate; we will have to bring it down. But just the same, among all the OECD countries Canada has by far the best record in terms of job creation.
If it were just a simple matter of jobs and inflation, perhaps we could solve all our problems locally, and perhaps even the Tories could handle it; they probably could manage. But the scene is not just a simple matter of inflation or creating jobs; the interplay between inflation and the creation of jobs is a problem. If we do the things we really need to do to bring the unemployment rate down to 2 per cent or 3 per cent, we will seriously affect the inflation aspect; and if we let inflation go too far, we will create more unemployment.
We have serious problems in these areas, but I think we must talk about other areas. For instance, we must talk about the world resource scene and particularly the energy scene. I am not speaking in terms of amounts of BTUs lying around but, rather, in terms of the financial aspect. We have about seven years' reserves of crude oil in the western basin. There are very improbable supplies in the north and on the offshore islands. There is nothing to speak of, or nothing which is worth going after. There are growing shortages of gas.
