speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
You tell me where these supplies are. We are not going to be self-sufficient in the next few years, or perhaps more. There are some supplies in the tar sands, but the costs there are astronomical, and this is what I am here to talk about. I am not talking about the total situation in terms of energy, because there always was energy, but I am talking about the energy which must be put in and the dollars which

October 15, 1976
The Address-Mr. McRae
must be put in to get the energy out. That is where we are going to be in trouble.
Last spring it was estimated-I heard a much higher estimate recently-that in the next 15 years we will need over $180 billion of capital just to maintain a 3.5 per cent energy growth rate. If we drop below that, of course, we will not need that amount of money. That $180 million, amortized in any reasonable fashion, would mean that we are talking about $3,000 per family unit, roughly what a family now pays for a house per year, in today's dollars. These are some of the problems. Where are we going to get that $180 billion capital plus another $400 billion or $500 billion capital which we need for other things? Just to increase the money supply or to play around with fiscal policy will not provide solutions. This is far more complex than people realize, and I think it is up to members of this House, on the government side and on the opposition side, to consider these problems seriously and not just criticize.
We have some very severe balance of payments problems. Our balance of payments current account is running about $5 billion in the red. There are those who say that foreign capital is a great thing and I agree. It built this country, but it still costs us close to $3 billion per year to service that capital. We are running about $43 billion in the red, in net terms. That is the money we owe to other countries. These are some of the things we have to face.
Then there is another very bad international scene-a very difficult international scene for any government to come to grips with. There has been a tremendous increase in the number and size of global corporations and the amount of liquid assets that are beyond the call of national governments. The United States Senate finance committee calculated that in 1973 these assets were between $150 billion and $260 billion, and that the total assets of global corporations were W2 to 2 times the size of the total liquid assets of national governments and their national banks, and that these liquid assets were able to move very rapidly; they had a great deal more mobility than the assets of national banks or even of groups like the International Monetary Fund.
There was the problem of the whole trend of worldwide inflation being changed because of the mobility of the assets of the global corporations. One can look at the descent of the pound sterling and ask to what extent is the inability of the International Monetary Fund and the inability of the national banks to control the movement of funds responsible.
I point out these facts to show that there are very complex problems that must be dealt with. There are no simple answers, and the answers that might have worked in the sixties do not work today. I ask opposition parties to start dealing with these problems and not just watch the Gallup polls or just criticize without offering solutions.
When we say that controls may be a bad thing, or say that we should get out of controls, we should look at what might happen when they end. We should look not only at the
[Mr. McRac.l
problem of inflation but at all the other factors which are difficult to control. I say these are very complex times, Mr. Speaker. Now is not the time to be negative; it is the time for all of us to start looking for solutions.
I should like to take the last five minutes or so of my time to speak about the role of the Department of National Health and Welfare and to make one or two comments on the Speech from the Throne and what the department will be doing with respect to the provinces. I should like to comment on the initiatives being taken by this government to map out and institute new and innovative financial and administrative arrangements between the federal and the provincial governments in the areas of medical insurance, hospital insurance and post-secondary education.
These programs have developed on the basis of open-ended cost-sharing arrangements whereby the federal government effectively matched the expenditures by provinces. The key word is "open-ended". This was an effective means to encourage the development of these programs and to make them available on a Canada-wide basis. There have been some difficulties, however, as the provinces have had problems restraining program costs in fields where a dollar of expenditure automatically generates 50 cents of additional federal contributions.
As a result of the problems in constraining costs under open-ended cost-sharing, the federal government has had to impose limits on the rate of increase of federal contributions to medical care-as we did with Bill C-68-and to post-secondary education and has served notice that the agreements under hospital insurance will come to an end in 1980. All of these actions have complicated provincial planning for the future as they are uncertain about the future level of federal participation in these programs.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) outlined to the provinces at the June 14-15, 1976, conference of first ministers a broad new approach for providing federal contributions to the major shared-cost programs. Under this proposal the federal government will continue to pay a substantial share of the medical insurance, hospital insurance and post-secondary education program costs. But the federal contribution will be paid in a manner that does not distort provincial priorities, that will encourage the provinces to effect cost constraint in these programs, and will not involve the federal government in open-ended spending commitments. Fundamentally, the established programs' financing arrangement would determine the federal government contribution independent of provincial program expenditures and on a basis that would result in greater equality in the per capita contribution made to the provinces by the federal government.
This movement away from open-ended cost-sharing for these established programs will substantially improve this government's ability to plan its own expenditure. At the same time, the provinces will have much greater flexibility in the use of their own funds and in the planning of their programs. For example, in the health field there will no longer be concern about whether or not a particular health service is shareable.
October 15, 1976

This added flexibility will assist them in providing the most appropriate and cost-efficient system of health services for Canadians.
A much more detailed outline of the principles and structure of the established programs' financing proposal is contained in the Prime Minister's statement presented to the provinces at the meeting referred to earlier. I should like to add several comments that are of particular relevance to the federal government's involvement in the health field.
Under established programs' financing there will continue to be a substantial federal contribution to health program costs and a substantial component of this contribution will be in the form of cash. In addition, and I should like to stress this point, there will continue to be basic health insurance program objectives of the type currently used for medical care embodied in replacement federal health legislation. These objectives are-and I have taken this reference directly from the Prime Minister's statement-comprehensiveness of coverage with regard to services; universality of coverage with regard to people; portability of benefits; accessibility to services uninhibited by excessive user charges, and non-profit administration by a public agency. It is intended that these basic program objectives will be retained within a more flexible and less administratively detailed federal-provincial financial arrangement than currently exists.
Second, I should like to comment on the timing for the full involvement of the health programs under established programs' financing. The current agreements for hospital insurance between the two orders of government are not scheduled to terminate until 1980. If the provinces wish to retain these agreements until that time, the health programs will not be fully brought under established programs' financing until this government's obligations under the hospital insurance agreements have been fulfilled. There is no danger of our going out of it until the date when the programs come to an end. It was clear, because of the variety of termination dates for the major shared-cost programs, that there would have to be a gradual introduction of the new financial and administrative arrangements.
Finally, with respect to the health field, it should be noted that this government will continue to pursue policies which attack some of the underlying causes of ill health in Canada. We will continue to encourage Canadians to adopt a lifestyle that maintains their good health. Operation Lifestyle, and information to discourage the excessive use of alcohol, are examples of steps that this government is taking to promote the retention of good health by Canadians.
In summary, it is the intent of this government to map out and begin to institute during this session a new financial and administrative arrangement for medical insurance, hospital insurance and post-secondary education. The established programs' financing proposal will both facilitate cost constraint and will provide the provinces with the necessary flexibility to provide appropriate but cost-efficient health and post-secondary education programs.
The Address-Mr. McKinnon
I should like to conclude my remarks by reiterating our concern about open-ended cost programs, about government expenditures, about the health of Canadians, about preventive medicine, about preventive health care, which we think is extremely important, and to mention some of the proposed programs such as the anti-alcohol program.
I should also like to ask all members of the House, regardless of their party, to be much more thoughtful when looking at Canada's economic future, to be much more thoughtful in terms of the very basic problems this country has to face and, to be more thoughtful in terms of understanding the limits to which any government of this country can go; given this kind of understanding of, for instance, the great shortage of capital that is going to face us in the next 15 years, I ask hon. members to move ahead with a real effort to explain to the people of Canada the complexities of these times. We should explain that we are not dealing with the relatively simple times of the sixties, but with complex problems of the seventies which will not be solved without a great deal of assistance from all concerned and more understanding on the part of the Canadian people.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I join with my colleagues in expressing congratulations to the mover and seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, the hon. member for Restigouche (Mr. Harquail) and the hon. member for Lafontaine-Rosemont (Mr. Lachance). They deserve a compliment for their courage in supporting a document as empty as the Speech from the Throne.
I listened with great interest to the previous speaker, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. McRae). Having listened to his economic theories, I am of opinion that he might have written that part of the throne speech which examined the alternatives and came down clearly between two stools, in a surprising show of clairvoyance on behalf of the government.
I compliment those who made it to the cabinet for the first time. The appointees from British Columbia unfortunately seem not to have made it to the first rung of the ladder; they are half way up to the first rung. The duties of the new Minister of State responsible for amateur sport (Mrs. Cam-pagnolo) seem to be somewhat divided. One part consists of being a hired pistol for the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde); the other of being a campaigner in British Columbia. It is known as being underemployed, considering the ability the hon. member has shown in her previous position as parliamentary secretary.
Before I talk about my usual subject, defence, I want to mention something concerning health and welfare which the parliamentary secretary and the Minister of State responsible for fitness and amateur sport both left out of their speeches. The omission was glaring. I am referring to the reciprocity of pensions.
Last April 14, six months and one day ago, the Minister of National Health and Welfare saw fit to rise in his place and,

October 15, 1976
The Address-Mr. McKinnon
in a speech filled with his usual, fulsome self-praise, stated that he wished to announce the government's intention to submit to parliament in the coming months legislation amending the Old Age Security Act. According to the minister, parliament would be asked to adopt measures, to build into our program the possibility for the inclusion of rights in international reciprocal arrangements with other countries such as Italy, the United States, and the United Kingdom, so that our residents who have earned social security rights in other countries can receive them in Canada. Last Wednesday, as reported at page 19 of Hansard, the minister, answering the question of my colleague from Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), said that the bill to negotiate reciprocity of pensions between Canada and several other countries, including the United Kingdom, is being drafted. He said:
... I hope I will be able to table it in the House for first reading in the next few months.
Six months ago he hoped to prepare the bill in the next few months; now, six months later, he hopes to be ready for first reading in the next few months. Even more alarming was the minister's answer to the supplementary question of the hon. member for Hamilton West. He said:
This project was discussed with my colleagues, if I remember well, at the last federal-provincial conference held in June, and no objection was made to the project either at the June conference or afterwards. Consequently, I think that we can undertake with confidence a study of this project.
That is what the minister said, as reported at page 19 of Hansard. What on earth was he talking about? Six months ago he said he would bring in a bill in a few months. Six months later he is still to bring in the same bill in a few months. Then he said that he thinks "we can undertake with confidence a study of this project."
In his fulsome speech of April 14 the minister said that this provision was going to affect, I think, half a million Canadians. Now he is ignoring those half a million Canadians and putting them on the shelf to cool, while he studies the project. Among those affected are tens of thousands of Canadians who are existing in distressed circumstances on British and other European pensions. Remember, the sole source of income for many of those elderly citizens is their British pension. In the last two months the pound has dropped drastically. This has meant a direct cash cutback for them on each month's cheque. Conditions for them are impossible. They have waited patiently for the past three months for parliament to reconvene.
I assumed, as any reasonable person well might, that the Minister of National Health and Welfare, having had the months of the summer in which to prepare a bill, would, as his first action, present it for first reading. That has not been the case. I hope the minister will think this over and try to relieve as quickly as possible the distress of those who have become innocent victims of his procrastination.
As we know, another cabinet minister has resigned. I am speaking of the former minister of national defence. I was concerned in case the departure of the minister meant the end of the financing arrangements he had been able to wrest from a reluctant cabinet for increasing the capital budget of the

Department of National Defence. I was pleased to note that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), when answering my question two days ago, affirmed that these increases would not be cut back, but would continue. We will look forward to seeing the estimates of the Department of National Defence come down either in December or January.
Today we are without a minister of national defence, although I understand there is an acting minister who is not in the House today. Presumably the parliamentary secretary could, to a limited extent, answer questions on behalf of the minister. As lamentable as this situation is, it is by no means inconsistent with the conduct of the country's defence policy. Lack of foresight, the absence of any concern for the long-run consequences of their actions, indeed a general unwillingness to discuss or even think about the future of the forces in any terms except platitudes-all these approaches have characterized the Liberals' national defence "non-policies".
To deduce what the government intends to do with the forces we thus have little to go on, save what we can extrapolate from past actions. Let us turn then to look at the sorry events of the past decade and examine them for any consistency of approach in the decisions on defence. The past decade has been one of marked change in government. There has been a veritable explosion in its growth; by any measure the money collected by the government, the size of the civil service, government expenditures as a percentage of GNP-government as a whole has become large, almost beyond recognition.
There has, however, been one salient exception to this tendency toward expansion; this same decade has seen the contraction, undermining and, indeed, virtual destruction of a major part of the capabilities of the Canadian Armed Forces. While the Trudeau administration has been responsible for this vast expansion of federal spending, its considered policy seems to have been to run down the forces and their equipment by quietly denying them the resources necessary for their continued existence as effective fighting forces.
The process which caused this contraction is no secret. The defence budget was held close to a constant figure during a period of ever-increasing inflation; the consequence was a defence budget which shrank in absolute terms. The result was a drastic reduction in manpower, from 110,000 in 1966 to 78,000 in 1976. What is not so well known is the way in which the government's short-run opportunism caused the Department of National Defence to misallocate its long-term resources. Not being privy to the government's long-term plans, DND tried to protect its manpower at the expense of weapons procurement even when much of its equipment was clearly approaching the end of its useful life.
Now we can look at the cabinet's handiwork and see what a sorry waste of resources DND was forced into by this hesitant and disastrous policy of bringing the forces down to their present level, without ever having the political courage or simple honesty to tell the Canadian armed forces and the country back in 1966 that the total strength would be drasti-
October 15, 1976

cally reduced by 1976. If the truth had been told then, so many defence dollars spent on the long rearguard action to conserve manpower and bases could have been switched into the capital budget; thus obsolescent equipment could have been replaced at the proper time.
The purchase of equipment could have been spread over the last decade, equipment which would now be in service providing new teeth for the maintenance of our national sovereignty and of our commitments to our allies. Instead we are facing the prospect of having to pay a huge bill for replacing virtually all of our major weapon systems now, over the space of just a few fiscal years.
Even if the government denies that it was its deliberate intention to starve DND of its ability to invest in weapons for the future, it must agree that it was foolish and failed to provide for the future by a proper investment policy. Any businessman or manager worth his job could have told it that with 63 per cent of the annual defence budget going to pay and allowances, 26 per cent to maintenance and operations, and only 11 per cent to capital expenditures, as it did in Canada in 1972, there would be trouble. The Liberals' short term political expediency has indeed cost the forces dearly.
Yet 1972 was the year after "the defence review", a review produced with the usual fanfare of a Trudeau media event, and published in the form of a white paper, "Defence in the Seventies." We can see now what this performance was really all about. It was a phenomenon which Trudeau-watchers should know so well by now, the mere facade of a policy, launched amid a blitz of glossy PR work, of "meaningful" briefings, a supposed re-ordering of priorities, and carefully leaked anecdotes about Prime Ministerial decisiveness.
Well, as we all know, that is all we get. The review itself is the only action that takes place. After the maximum publicity has been reaped, the Prime Minister and his team-that inner group whose numbers, like inflation, have soared during the last decade-take off for pastures new, leaving the ministerial "fall guy" to the gradual realization that this is it. The officials and the minister have the dubious privilege of picking up the pieces, salvaging what is left of their commitments, and measuring the gaps between them and their inadequate resources.
So "Defence in the Seventies" was a public relations front, a fa9ade behind which the Trudeau cabinet could cut DND's budget in real terms and emasculate it as an effective force.
Quite suddenly last year the policy appeared to have been changed. The then minister was suddenly heard everywhere in the land promising new equipment and the money to buy it. However, it is also very noticeable that no other minister, let alone the Prime Minister, has been heard to say anything in public in support of the commitment to re-equip the armed forces. Why is this so? The answer is that the Liberal cabinet may have promised new weapons, but its members' hearts are not in it. Let me suggest that this is because they do not really feel that DND should have the money. They have not suddenly become converts to a proper defence policy for Canada. On the contrary, one has to look in some surprising places for the real
The Address-Mr. McKinnon
reasons for their sudden interest in defence, and these reasons are hardly calculated to fill the country with confidence that the Liberal government is fulfilling its obligations to provide for the security of this country.
We should all ask ourselves why the Prime Minister has suddenly become interested in NATO, interested beyond the ritual mouthing of support which he has previously given his allies. The only past actions of his concerning NATO which come to mind are the decisions to cut the Canadian manpower contribution by half, and not to replace the aging Centurion tank.
Yet recently we have a new found enthusiasm for tanks, and we have all witnessed the tragic comedy caused by the previous minister of national defence's precipitous haste to announce a contract for the LRPA. So precipitous was the haste to announce the first LRPA contract that cabinet did not even give it the attention one might expect from any group of responsible adults about to spend a billion dollars. But then what was another billion to a cabinet which asked so few questions about a company like Lockheed that its members signed an agreement without even bothering to read the briefing notes prepared for them by their own officials?
Why should the NATO commitments suddenly appeal to the Prime Minister? The answer is not any perception of an increased Soviet threat; that right hon. gentleman appears not to be even dimly aware of the upgrading of Soviet tactical land, sea and air forces. Anyway, he barely bothers to conceal his contempt for such military matters. He certainly feels it beneath his dignity to make a speech about them.
The latest comment I have heard from his lips was that, when speaking of the former minister of national defence retaining his portfolio, he had bought Jim his new toys and he should stay on and play as minister of national defence.
No, the Prime Minister is interested in NATO because he was left in no doubt that, if he wanted his "contractual link" with the European Economic Community, a precondition of a favourable deal was to end his shameful neglect of the equipment needs of the Canadian Armed Forces. A sad state of affairs has surely come to pass when foreign governments care more for Canada's Armed Forces than does the Trudeau cabinet.
The LRPA deal has been signed. The contract is now being put into effect. I have very few comments to make on that. I wish the company well. I hope they survive to the end of the contract. Canadians should hold their breath for the next four or five years until we get the aircraft for which we are going to pay so dearly.
It is interesting to note that when the then minister of national defence failed to get cabinet approval in May, it was given over to the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) to close the deal. He did this with the usual fanfare and, with his usual business acumen, was able to see that a plane priced at $953 million in December could be bought at a different price because it had a lot less on it and he would only have to pay an extra $60 million for it. Having watched that same
126

October 15, 1976
The Address-Mr. McKinnon
gentleman buy oil at $1 a gallon and not be able to sell it for 15 cents a gallon, one should not be surprised.
The new long-range patrol aircraft is an inferior plane compared to the one for which the then minister of national defence attempted to get approval. It has less instrument landing capability. The November plane could land in conditions of 100-foot ceiling and one-quarter mile visibility. The new plane, which costs $60 million more, needs double that minimum.
Second, the bomb-bay canisters are no longer going to be part of the contract. They provide, in their words, a unique sovereignty, surveillance, research and civilian sensing capability. This has now gone by the board.
The data annotation system on the new plane is of inferior quality compared to the one on what we might now call the Richardson aircraft. The electronic emission detection system on the new plane is not up to that on the old one. The system on the new plane is "capable of growth to a more advanced system".
Finally, and perhaps most different, is the data interpretation and analysis centres. There were to be two, one at Greenwood, and one at Comox. Now there will be one at Greenwood. The one at Comox is not to be of the same quality or standard as the one at Greenwood. It is to be a D1AC with a reduce capability. This capability is yet to be defined. This means we know what we are going to pay, but we do not know what we are going to get. By the time we pay for the canisters, the upgrading of the Comox facility and anything else we decide to restore to its former capability, the bill will be far beyond the currently stated price.
I wish now to say a few words about tanks. A couple of years ago the then minister of national defence and the Prime Minister discovered tanks were no longer needed and they were going out of the tank business. But following their conversion by the Chancellor of Germany they decided it would not be too bad an idea to re-equip the Canadian forces with tanks. I would remind hon. members that they had totally spurned an opposition initiative and suggestion in committee about a year ago that they should consider renting tanks while deciding what tanks to order. They suddenly changed their minds and decided that this was a good idea and they are now arranging to rent German tanks for up to two years. I welcome this idea. Indeed, I suggested it.
I now further suggest that before getting into a contract to buy Leopard I tanks, they should bear in mind that at least 19 prototypes of Leopard II have been constructed and the new version is about to come on the market. It will be superior in many respects to the Leopard I. What worries me is that we are now proposing to buy the Leopard I just at a time when it is the last off the line, in other words, the last of a series. Almost instantly we shall be using a new obsolescent tank.
One of the important factors is that the Leopard II will be equipped with a 120mm gun. The Leopard I carries a 105mm gun. The Warsaw Pact countries are currently operating a

tank which is impervious to attack by a 105mm gun and for this reason, if for no other, I would ask the new minister to check into the possibility of buying the Leopard II instead of the Leopard I, or at least the possibility of having the 120mm weapon retro-fitted into the Leopard I.
A similar lack of foresight is involved in another new commitment, one which any responsible cabinet would have seen coming for the last two or three years at least. This is the extension of our economic zone to 200 miles offshore. As from the New Year these responsibilities will fall on some department or departments. The government is silent as to which will be assuming responsibility for the role of co-ordinating offshore operations. This being the case, the Canadian taxpayer must assume that, as usual, either the government doesn't know or is as muscle-bound as ever with committees, task forces, inter-departmental studies and so on, all of which are producing mounds of paper, but there is not one responsible politician who can get something going in time to be ready for the declaration of sovereignty. There is absolutely no sign of any extra funds forthcoming to meet the equipment, manpower, or operating costs which will be necessary to fulfil this new commitment.
Since the various agencies of government do not have the funds to enable them to carry out proper fisheries patrols in the much smaller area of sea currently claimed, we shall shortly be witnessing yet another example of a tired, worn out cabinet failing to reach any decision except that most common Liberal decision, the non-decision or decision by default.
Recently the minister and senior officers of the forces have taken to claiming that a shipbuilding program does exist. We have heard mention of a 20-year program; we have heard mention of 20 ships in 20 years. A general officer touring in Germany recently published an article in Kanadaire the service newspaper there, to claim that there was a shipbuilding program. Having heard these stories, I put a question on the order paper on July 6, question No. 5,479. It is reported in Hansard at page 15076 as follows:
1.	Has the Department of National Defence set up a planning section or any other type of unit, section or project office to carry out planning and procurement of the 20 new ships announced by the minister and, if so, how many (a) servicemen (b) civilians are so employed?
2.	What is the amount of money allocated for this purpose for the fiscal year 1976-77?
In his reply the former minister of national defence said:
No. Although no specific announcement about procurement of 20 new ships has been made, planning studies for ship replacement continue to be carried out by departmental staff as part of their regular duties.
He went on to say that parts (a) and (b) were not applicable, and that the answer to the second part of the question
was "Nil". So much for Liberal promises about re-equipping our fleet.
To sum up, after a decade of neglect and cuts in defence spending we now find ourselves in a situation where we must race to catch up for the lost years and lost equipment dollars. Due to the negligence of successive defence ministers in the Trudeau era we must suddenly spend a disproportionate

October 15, 1976

amount from the federal budget on defence during the next few fiscal years. If the first effort, the LRPA debacle, is anything to go by, the House cannot allow the government to proceed any further with major procurement decisions affecting our defence policy for the next 20 years for this is how long the new weapons will have to last without a much fuller examination of its policy. Not only must we be told many more details concerning any future contracts but we must also make sure we buy the right items of equipment for the right price in the proper order of priority. Clearly the ministers who have been involved in such matters in the past proved incapable of handling them.
In the past several months there has been a continuing review during which the military and civilian officers of the defence department have sought to work out these questions. However, only the cabinet is privy to the information which is supplied from these sources. In the name of security and official secrecy the taxpayers, especially their elected representatives in this House, are denied such information.
At hearings of the Defence Committee which examines the estimates this problem was revealed at its most acute. Senior officials of the department were prevented from outlining even the broadest picture of future costs and priorities following the doctrine that once a policy had been submitted to cabinet for consideration they were not free to discuss it with members of parliament. On the other hand, if a subject had not yet reached the stage at which a firm proposal had been made for cabinet consideration, the officials refused, as they put it, to "speculate" except in a most general-and therefore pretty useless-way. One might be forgiven for believing that this practice was designed to deny information to the House. In any case the result is that the options for future defence arrangements which have been given to the cabinet have been denied to the public.
One consequence of this, of course, is that the military and others whose views the cabinet ignores tend to leak their plans to the press, partly no doubt because of the government's own use of this channel of communication. What we need is a new quorum or method of formalizing a proper debate on defence without endangering security.
A good example is the study which was conducted with regard to the closing of bases. This study was first mentioned last winter. Word spread that the government was considering the closing of several bases in the interests of rationalization. Question after question was asked in the House, and invariably the minister of national defence stonewalled, saying that the survey was under study by the cabinet and he was therefore not free to discuss the matter. We continued to press for answers, and then a strange press leak in July or August indicated that the study was no longer a current issue-no bases were to be closed. The whole thing was to be forgotten. This was followed, two days later, by a denial from the department. The matter was still under consideration by the cabinet-don't hold your breath waiting for the final answer. This leaves a terrible amount of uncertainty in the country.
The Address-Mr. Brewin
Such cities as Edmonton, Calgary and London all have major bases; none of them know whether their base is the one to be chopped. This uncertainty is even worse than the final act of closing a base. I would ask the minister either to announce a policy and tell us what bases are to be closed, or to tell us frankly that there is no intention to close any bases.
One other thing I should like to mention. The re-equipment policy has been moving very slowly ahead. I would like to put it clearly on the record that the Conservative party believes that up to the present the Department of National Defence has not made a clear case with respect to the replacement of CF-101 Voodoo fighters. We are in favour of all other aspects of the re-equipment program.
My party supports, and incidentally has been doing so for rather longer than the present government, the need for new tanks, armoured personnel carriers, the replacement of the CF-104 Star Fighter in the ground support role, the long-range patrol aircraft and, not least, a new naval shipbuilding program. Those are things supported by myself and my party, and I want that clearly understood.
Finally I should like to say I had the pleasure this summer of visiting our peacekeeping forces on Cyprus and in the Middle East. All Canadians can be extremely proud of the very fine job they are doing out there under very difficult circumstances. They are tremendous troops and are capably led. I am sure General Clay Beattie is considered by Cypriots on both side of the demarcation line as being really the peacemaker and the peacekeeper on Cyprus. Anyone who would wish to discourage peacekeeping should compare the state that Cyprus is in with the state Lebanon is in. Lebanon does not have a peacekeeping force but Cyprus does.
While in Cyprus I had the privilege of being the guest of the PPCLI, a very fine regiment indeed-none better in the world, I submit. I wish to express my thanks for the courtesy and treatment I received from Lieutenant Colonel Gollner and his very fine battalion.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is not infrequently my fate to address the House on Friday afternoon. I should like to say to those who are present that I am reminded of the minister who, on a rainy day, said to the rather sparse congregation that he had the quality if not the quantity of his congregation with him. I think I can say that to the hon. members of the House who are with us still.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Particularly looking forward.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House in its wisdom has provided that the Speech from the Throne gives an opportunity for discussing any problems affecting the welfare of Canada. I therefore make no apology for directing my speech to the sphere of international affairs. However important our domestic problems are, and I know they are important, they are no more important to the future security and welfare of Canadi-
80001-9]/2

October 15, 1976
The Address-Mr. Brewin
ans than the global inter-dependence which is an increasing fact of life.
It is no accident that questions such as survival in a nuclear age, food, health, population, the rights of women, and the problems of the environment have all been subjects for international conferences under the auspices of the United Nations, and at all of these conferences the view emerged that international action was required if solutions were to be found. One can add to this list the subject of inflation which is, after all, not purely a national phenomenon.
The first item in the international situation I should like to deal with is the immense mal-distribution of the resources of the world, both material and personal. It is estimated that the world is spending a figure of over $300 billion a year on arms. The world bank was asked to make an estimate of what it would cost to make the basic investments required to deal with certain fundamental obstacles, and it came up with the following figure: food and nutrition, $42 billion; education, $25 billion; rural and urban water supply, $28 billion; urban housing, $16 billion; urban transport, $8 billion; population and health programs, $6 billion, amounting in all to roughly $125 billion over ten years, or about $12.5 billion a year. I would ask you to compare those figures with the 10-year figure for arms expenditure which is expected to be at least $2,500 billion in the next ten years.
Proposals have been made to remedy this gross and insane misspending of resources. The Pope proposed at the World Food Conference a diversion of 10 per cent of arms expenditures to development aid. The Soviet Union, which is one of the main players in the lunatic game of over-kill and first strike capability, has also proposed a 10 per cent cut in arms, the savings to be transferred to development aid. Barbara Ward in her book "The Home of Man" repeats the proposal. It is my suggestion that Canada take up this proposal seriously and undertake to make its contribution of a 10 per cent cut in arms expenditures to be transferred to development and to meeting the basic needs of mankind, and to persuade other nations to do the same.
I referred to the Soviet proposal, which was responded to with a resounding silence. One is perhaps entitled to be skeptical about the bona fide intentions of a country devoted to arms expenditures such as the USSR. However, if it is a bluff the bluff should be called.
The former minister of national defence was obviously elated when he apparently persuaded the Cabinet to agree that military expenditures should not only keep up with the cost of living but should increase by 12 per cent a year. I suggest that his resignation gives an opportunity for reconsideration. There is no more inflationary an expenditure than spending on arms. It is not necessary in order to provide Canada's needs for defence, defence of her sovereignty, and to give priority to peacekeeping consistent with Canada's aims and objectives, to spend the amount of money that is being spent. I am well aware that there will be people in the House, as there are in the country, who will say that this proposal has no popular appeal. I think they are quite right. We have been conditioned

to think of defence expenditure as sacrosanct. When one considers what could be done with the rearrangement of expenditures as suggested, namely, the proposal made of cutting 10 per cent of arms expenditure and applying it to development, it is in fact, counsel of sanity in a world that might otherwise drift toward self-destruction.
A second priority in Canada's international policy should be practical support for the new economic order. Canada is indeed committed to making the new economic order a reality and this commitment was referred to, albeit in rather vague terms, in the Speech from the Throne. I suggest that the importance of this cannot be exaggerated. World instability has resulted from gross inequalities between developed and developing countries. Developing countries entered on a path of confrontation demanding trade concessions and a change of structures in the world's economic system. They are now testing the developed world to see if it is ready to choose the path of co-operation and social justice.
In this connection I should like to pay tribute to the former secretary of state for external affairs. He was co-chairman at the North-South Conference in Paris at which positive solutions were being sought. I remind the House that a committee of this House in the last session studied thoroughly the matter of developing a new economic order and gave its support in practical terms to the liberalization of trade and greater stability of prices for goods sold by developing countries. To this end it proposed that a common fund should be set up for the purpose of creating buffer stocks and stabilizing prices. At the recent UNCTAD conference at Nairobi the Canadian government finally came up with a cautious approval of this project.
I hope the new Secretary for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson), whom I congratulate on his appointment, will as soon as possible tell the House in detail what is proposed by the government on the whole question of the new economic order, the common fund, and commodity prices, and of developments at the North-South Economic Co-operative Conference. These questions cannot be solved by rhetoric alone. We have had plenty of that. They require action.
A third subject which I wish to discuss is the proliferation of nuclear weapons manufactured out of plutonium which can be produced in reactors sold by Canada. This was discussed in the last session, and the Conservative and New Democratic opposition parties voted against the sale of reactors under the existing circumstances. The case against these sales grows stronger and stronger. The leader of this party the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent), proposed that the whole question of the production of nuclear energy be the subject of an inquiry by experts in the field, to be made public to the people of Canada, and that until such an inquiry had reported there be a moratorium on the sale of nuclear reactors or other material capable of being turned into nuclear bombs.
Recently a royal commission in Great Britain reported on this subject. They urged the necessity for wide public under-
October 15, 1976

standing and the need for public debate. They proposed that a major commitment to fission power should be postponed as long as possible, and that a commitment to large nuclear programs should wait until there has been wide public understanding of the implications of a plutonium economy.
In particular they urged that a high level body be established in Great Britain to provide advice on energy and to enable more research to be put into alternative solutions. In connection with the so-called plutonium economy they drew specific attention to the dangers of plutonium being used by terrorists to blackmail society and the small amounts required for the making of nuclear bombs. I join my leader and many others throughout Canada who have urged a moratorium on the sale of reactors for distribution as potential sources of extracting plutonium until a thorough inquiry has been made. Prestigious voices in the United States have supported this proposal for a moratorium, including David Lilienthal, former chairman of the Tennessee Valley Authority and an expert in the whole field of energy.
I myself have recently had an experience which demonstrates the need for caution. One of the countries to which we are proposing to sell one or two reactors is the Argentine. I and two of my colleagues, the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald), and the hon. member for Montmorency (Mr. Duclos), recently returned from a trip to the Argentine. There could be little doubt about the instability of that country.
A military dictatorship has deprived Argentinians of their human rights; trade unions are virtually non-existent; the church and other institutions are under attack; many individuals are detained without trial; roughly 1,000 have totally disappeared and their families are unable to obtain any information about them. Shootings and assassinations are a daily event. The authorities in the Argentine do not deny that this state of disorder exists. They blame it on leftist guerillas. There seems to be widespread agreement among others that, in addition to left-wing guerillas, the "death squad" consists of right-wing elements who are determined to repress not only left-wing ideas but any democratic institutions which might be a source of opposition.
The government appears to be either unwilling or unable to control these terrorist gangs. While there is a vigorous campaign by the government to deal with left-wing guerillas no similar effort is made to restrain the right wing elements responsible, at the present time, for most of the disappearances and killings which have taken place. This has created an unstable society and one in which if the terrorists could secure plutonium and manufacture nuclear bombs, these could be used both within and outside the Argentine as a weapon of blackmail. As I said, the government authorities did not deny the breaches of human rights but justified this on the basis that a state of war existed. The Argentine has not signed the nuclear non-proliferation agreement, and although Canada has arranged for certain safeguards as a condition of sale, the safeguards are just as good as the recipients choose to make them.
The Address-Mr. Brewin
We cannot enforce these safeguards. There are no effective sanctions. If governments or groups within the Argentine decide to disregard them, the threat of the misuse of nuclear weapons might spread among the nations of the world, and this is a threat to the survival of all of us. Canada should think again on this subject.
The central issue in the world today consists of developments in Africa. We must continue to hope for and assist in any way possible the granting of majority rule in Zimbabwe, but that is only part of the problem. There remains the continuing illegal occupation of Namibia, formerly German Southwest Africa, by South Africa. This situation flies in the teeth of the judgment of the world as expressed in United Nations resolutions. It will have to come to an end and should be ended by negotiations giving full independence to the majority, who consist of black Africans.
Another problem is the continuing curse of apartheid in South Africa itself. This evil system cannot continue indefinitely. There is one immediate development with which I wish to deal, and that is the effort of South Africa to obtain recognition from Canada and other countries for the so-called Republic of Transkei. This proposal is a patent fraud. Transkei is to be declared independent and made the national home of all Xhosa-speaking Africans. The Transkei's present population of about 1.7 million in a crowded, poor, and sparse country would increase to around 3 million.

I think our government should make up its mind by then and clearly declare what is its policy and decision on this matter.

The Address-Mr. Ouellet

Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes at my disposal during this throne speech debate, I wish to refer to three measures that I should like to see implemented during this session. First, I want the injustice done to many industrial milk producers in Canada to be corrected as soon as possible. Second, in agreement with the provinces, I should like the federal government to patriate the Canadian constitution as soon as possible. Third, I wish it were possible between responsible parliamentarians to amend our rules of parliamentary proceedings which are obsolete in many ways and provide us with ancient tools to work with in these modern times.
First, with regard to the farm policy, the national dairy program as we know it has serious deficiencies. In many circles, the federal government is held responsible for the disastrous financial situation of a number of industrial milk producers in Canada. First, those affected are those who had their quotas cut down by some 20 per cent without any overproduction and also those who were encouraged to overproduce after being promised quotas that they never obtained. It is true that in 1975, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) had asked the milk producers to increase their production. But, mind you, at the time the Minister of Agriculture was speaking of a 5 per cent production increase. Yet, production increased by 17 per cent. Who is responsible? I say that it is primarily the milk supply management committee which is made up of producers, of representatives of the provincial governments and the Canadian Dairy Commission. It is a committee of 23 members including 11 producers (members of the various Canadian dairy federations), 9 provincial representatives and 3 commissioners of the Canadian Dairy Commission.
Now, the Canadian milk supply management committee, which is responsible for production control, did not reduce the marketing quotas before April 1, 1976, even though they largely exceeded the Canadian demand. Now, this year, this committee reduced the quotas to the level of the Canadian demand, which automatically reduced materially in some cases the income of several milk producers. Can the federal government be held responsible for this situation? Before blaming it for everything, let us consider what happened in the past few years. Under the federal dairy policy, the target price of industrial milk was increased every year. In April 1973, it was $6.45 a hundredweight, then it went up to $8.50 in April 1974, to $11.02 in April 1975, and it stands at $11.45 since April 1976. This is a marked improvement for milk producers.
Furthermore, if we refer to the 1972-73 dairy year, we find that the federal subsidy was then $1.25 a hundredweight. In April 1973, it went up to $1.45 and later to $2.01. In 1974-75

October 15, 1976
The Address-Mr. Ouellet
it was increased twice: first to $2.30 and then to $2.56, and in the present dairy year, it went up to $2.66 a hundredweight.
Once again, there has been a clear effort on the part of the federal government to help milk producers. But, more important, I am pleased to say that when I was a minister in the Trudeau government, I was associated with the decision that the Trudeau government announced in April 1975 through the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan): a long term dairy policy would particularly provide for an indexation formula of the price of milk. As it happened it was in keeping with that formula that the price of indutrial milk has been fixed this year at $ 11.45 from $ 11.02 last year.
These are examples that show that the federal government does take into account the interests of Canadian milk producers and that it does understand their problems. 1 think that the present difficulties on the international markets are due particularly to weather conditions that were extremely favourable to milk production in 1975 and which resulted in excess production and also in lower consumption of dairy products in Canada, following the increase in costs.
Those are roughly the main reasons behind the problems of some milk producers. I am quite concerned by this situation which I think is very serious especially for a group of young producers whose average age is 30 and who, not more than five years ago, have established agricultural industries; they were asked to reduce their production by several hundred thousands of pounds of milk, and most of them have respected the quotas which were supposed to bring them some form of security. Most of these young people were trained in technological institutes and regional agricultural institutions; some have taken the courses given under the auspices of the agriculture minister of the province of Quebec. These young people have entered the field of industrialized agriculture, they have planned five-year or more than five-year programs and they have entered into important financial contracts now, the cutbacks announced during these recent months nearly smother them and create nearly irreparable damages.
One fears that if this condition is not amended as quickly as possible by the authorities responsible for the dairy policy, at the federal and provincial levels and by the dairy boards, some 30 per cent of the producers of industrial milk will have to disappear within two years, which would be extremely serious and would jeopardize the stability of an industry of import not only to Quebec but to the whole of Canada.
Therefore, we will have to take our responsibilities at the federal level although we are not directly and primarily involved in this situation and, as I have said before, it is no use playing politics with this issue and denounce the federal government as the main culprit. Provincial authorities and dairy boards must recognize their shortcomings and more particularly those who represent the milk producers on the various agricultural boards and agencies. The fact is that a number of these representatives, Mr. Speaker, were representing whole milk producers, which form an industry which is far richer far sounder and much better organized and which emphasized, in terms of quotas and subsidies, the benefits and interests of
[Mr. Ouellet.)
whole milk producers, and did so unfortunately at the expense of industrial milk producers.
I believe that, in the interest of our dairy industry as a whole, we will have to give guarantees to all producers as well as the assurance that the past benefits they gained will be maintained. And by this 1 mean to say that I believe it to be vital for the federal government to take the appropriate action to give back to some dairy producers the quotas that they lost in the last few months and to reinstate them in the position that they held with respect to their production level of 197475. I believe it is urgent that the government should set back the production quotas to the production level of 1974-75 by means of subsidies to all producers, who would then be treated fairly, and also that he should urgently redistribute subsidized production quotas to those dairy producers who have invested tremendous amounts of money with the promise of additional quotas or to those who, without having any overproduction, either because of fire or cattle disease, have seen their production fall considerably below their recommended and approved quota and who have had part of their quota removed even though they had fallen short.
Here are the suggestions that I should like to make. I believe that in the interest of the Canadian dairy industry, we should give our milk producers assurances of survival, dignity of life in the farming community. I believe that the future of Canadian consumers does make it essential for farm producers to be well protected and for their income to be guaranteed, otherwise dairy production will go down and we shall have to rely on imports to feed the people of Canada. And I am convinced that we would then pay more for our dairy products than at the present time.
Secondly, I would like to speak briefly to the constitutional issue and the repatriation of the Constitution. 1 am doing so today on this very special occasion when the Canadian government has paid tribute to a great Canadian, the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, and unveiled a monument in his honour in front of the Supreme Court of Canada building. You all know that in 1949, the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, then prime minister of Canada, asked the Canadian Parliament to adopt a petition through which it obtained from British Parliament the right to amend the Canadian Constitution except in certain more controversial areas, such as the rights and powers of provinces, the jurisdiction with respect to education, the official duality of languages, the length of Parliaments. This was called at the time, and indeed, it is still called the partial repatriation of the Constitution. I would like to quote this excerpt from a book written by a former federal minister, the Hon. J. W. Pickersgill, and 1 quote:
-the title of the book is "My Years with Louis St. Laurent" and I quote from page 113 as follows:
St. Laurent proposed that ... the Canadian parliament should seek from the British parliament an amendment to the British North America Act to do three things: I. to entrench the rights or privileges with respect to schools and the use of the English or the French language granted to any class of persons by the
October 15, 1976

constitution; 2. to give the parliament of Canada exclusive jurisdiction to amend the constitution, except with respect to the minority rights regarding schools and languages and except in relation to provincial jurisdiction or provincial rights or privileges; 3. to give the parliament of Canada jurisdiction as well to make amendments relating to the matters which were not within its exclusive jurisdiction, but to provide that no such amendment would come into effect unless and until it was enacted as law by the legislatures of all the provinces.

As everyone knows, the first two proposals have been approved by the Canadian Parliament, and those first two objectives sought by Mr. St. Laurent have been approved and have now been enacted.
But the last objective he had in mind at the time has not been achieved. It is somewhat unfortunate, because it is clear that part of our constitution has not been patriated. The formula put forward at the time by Mr. St. Laurent entailed serious hazards and dangers, for there would have been a general outcry. Further on in his book, on page 121, Mr. Pickersgill states:

If that had happened, Canada would have been spared, since 1949, the continuing humiliation of having to ask the parliament of another country to amend our fundamental law. St. Laurent's proposal that no amendment affecting provincial rights or provincial jurisdiction could be made without the approval of all provincial legislatures was perhaps too rigid; but in fact, since 1907 the British parliament has not been asked to make such an amendment without approval of all provincial authorities nor is it likely to be.
Mr. Pickersgill ended the chapter on this subject by saying:
In the end, St. Laurent's formula of 1949 may prove to be the solution. [Translation]
Mr. Speaker, here are some reflections on Canada's current situation. We are a nation with its constitution in another country. If we amend, that is if we patriate the constitution without an amendment formula, we will remain the only nation, not with an expatriated constitution, but with an unamendable constitution. Clearly, what is needed, both from the federal government and the provincial representatives, is goodwill to attain that vital goal, a truly Canadian constitution, a constitution that will be for us another great symbol of unity.
There was much talk about the Canadian flag. It was said that the flag was a divisive issue. The Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson, however, had the courage to give this nation a truly Canadian flag, despite protests from a few Progressive Conservatives and a few bigots. In my view, this Canadian flag is a token of unity in this country, and I believe the Right Hon. Pierre Elliott Trudeau will shortly demonstrate the same kind of courage as Mr. Pearson did, I believe he will give Canadians a truly Canadian constitution despite the protest from some Progressive Conservatives and some bigots. In this way, we will have a constitution we can proudly call our own, for the well-being of all Canadians.
And this much I can state: as a Quebecer, I have absolutely no fear of a Canadian constitution. I am certainly not afraid that such a constitution reduce in any way the rights and provileges already enjoyed by Quebecers. As for the utterance by certain Quebec quarters that the province of Quebec should
The Address-Mr. Coates
have more powers, 1 am not opposed to granting certain extra powers. But I insist on one condition: if ever Quebec is given extra powers, I want to be sure that the rights and privileges of Quebec MP's are not reduced. Because the Quebec MP's would then lose their true raison d'etre in Canada's Parliament, and we would soon enter into an associated state or special state situation, with second rate and second class Quebec MP's. That I want to prevent.
I will close my remarks, Mr. Speaker, on a third matter: parliamentary reform. We are speaking on this subject on a Friday afternoon. I find this inconceivable, since a vast majority of members of parliament who live in the remote corners of this country have to travel regularly every week-end to go and see their constituents in British Columbia, Newfoundland, Alberta and Prince Edward Island.
I think it is very important that we modify our parliamentary procedure in order to sit longer hours certain days of the week. The House should sit four days instead of five days a week. I am sure that there are a lot of ways in which we might improve the parliamentary procedure. After having studied the House procedure, a committee has made a series of recommendations. Our colleagues of the Quebec and Ontario provincial legislatures have attended committee meetings or a Liberal caucus and have made a series of very timely recommendations which, I hope, will be taken into consideration as soon as possible by Parliament.

I was impressed with the statements made today by the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe and the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) on the language issue. They made unemotional, sensible, realistic approaches to that policy, a policy Canadians will get when the Progressive Conservative party forms the government of Canada after the next general election.

Unemployment is increasing in Canada at a mile a minute. If we continue the way we are going now, one million people will be unemployed in this country by the end of the year. This condition will worsen with escalating energy costs. We have to sit down and work together. We must get the language issue out of the way so that people are not first concerned about an emotional issue, but about the bread and butter issues.
I wish to speak briefly on my part of .this country, Atlantic Canada. In 1968, the Prime Minister inspired the people of Atlantic Canada. He convinced them that he had their best interests at heart. He talked about regional economic disparity


and put in place the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. Millions of dollars were committed to that department in order to try to meet the hopes and aspirations of those in Atlantic Canada.
As I look at the unemployment statistics today and compare our area with the rest of Canada, even with the millions of dollars that were committed and with all the good intentions of the government, it has not worked out as well as hoped.
I do not fault the government for its good intentions, which I believe it has. I have always been willing to work with the government in trying to meet the hopes and aspirations of those in my area. I am going to suggest to the government how we might overcome some of the problems we are facing and some of the reasons why DREE is not working as well as it should.
I have no disagreement with the Prime Minister appointing Ministers of State. That is a realistic concept. A cabinet should be stratified because there are a great many difficult problems at different levels. Thirty people cannot come to an agreement as quickly as five or six. Therefore a stratified cabinet is the proper solution.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) and the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) are both here. They are deeply involved. I suggest it would be a wise decision to have a Minister of State appointed who would have one responsibility. That minister would look at every program designated to overcome regional disparity in Atlantic Canada. Following an indepth examination of those programs, he would then examine all government programs to see whether they are damaging the concept of the regional programs. Let me give an example.
The user-pay concept in transportation will destroy Atlantic Canada. There are no two ways about it. Transportation must be a development tool in Atlantic Canada if we are to overcome the disparity we face. The user-pay concept has never before been applied, and should not be applied now. Transportation has been and continues to be a curse to Atlantic Canada because we do not have the right kind of development policy.
The user-pay concept is not applied to the St. Lawrence Seaway which does not receive enough revenue from the tolls to pay the interest on its indebtedness. If that were to be put into effect on the Seaway, we might as well seal it off, as well as the whole St. Lawrence River, because there would not be a ship in the Great Lakes.
We must forget about the user-pay concept in transportation and have a realistic policy of development. We should use the railways for the development of both eastern and western Canada so that we can come closer to an equality of trade right across this nation. That is just one example.
Now consider energy rates. Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia are facing, and will continue to face, energy rates which are higher than in any other part of Canada. This is because
80001-10'/2
The Address-Mr. Coates
those provinces are almost totally committed to the use of offshore oil for the production of the energy they require. Unless they are given some form of short-term subsidy we shall find a noose has been tied around the necks of industries which were established in their present locations only after the expenditure of millions of dollars of taxpayers' money. Mr. Speaker, it is absurd to use taxpayers' dollars to establish an industry and then allow energy costs to escalate to a point at which those same industries are put into bankruptcy, which is exactly what will happen unless the federal government recognizes that short-term subsidies are the only assurance of the continuing viability of a great many industries in Atlantic Canada.
I could give other examples of cases where federal programs have destroyed the regional programs established earlier to overcome one or other aspect of regional disparity. Something has to be done about this situation, and the best way of doing it is to make one minister responsible for the overseeing of all these programs. Part of his job would be to call public attention to cases where there is a conflict between the national and the regional program and to stimulate public discussion as to the manner in which such conflicts could be resolved. In effect, he would allow a regional program to operate, in the first place, and continue to do the job it was supposed to do. This can be done, Mr. Speaker, as long as we take the people of the area into our confidence, as long as "made in Ottawa" programs which are later found to be unworkable in the maritimes are not pressed upon the people of the region. In so many cases one finds that they are unworkable because no one in the maritimes was consulted as to whether they were likely to work or not, or because people in Ottawa have no conception of what they are up against in the Atlantic area.
My leader has indicated that if the party to which I belong were in power today we would introduce a short term subsidy program for the benefit of the people of Atlantic Canada so that they would not be called upon to face the horrendous energy costs presently being charged, costs which are likely to rise even higher in the months ahead. Let me give hon. members an example of what is involved. There are people owning electrically-heated homes in Atlantic Canada who are paying more for their power than for their mortgages.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Some of them are losing their homes.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Many are losing their homes. Moreover those homes are unsaleable because nobody in Nova Scotia wants to buy an electrically-heated house today, so the owner is saddled with a house which he cannot sell and which he cannot afford to keep. Yet there was a period in which those home-owners were duped by advertising agencies associated with the power companies into buying electrically-heated homes under the impression that it was cheaper to heat them that way than by any other means. Well, they have found out by now that there is nothing cheap about those homes. Many of them are built in such a way that they can be heated only by electricity; it is not practical to convert them to oil heating or gas by putting in a furnace. Something should be done about this serious burden

October 15, 1976
The Address-Mr. Coates
which many people in my own province of Nova Scotia are being asked to carry today.
I am concerned about the government's attitude toward the development of Fundy tidal power. As the Minister of Manpower moves up the echelon of cabinet positions and gets closer to the top I hope he will see that greater impetus is given to the drive to utilize Fundy tidal power. The Minister of Finance was always a realistic and sympathetic proponent of Fundy tidal power, and I hope that with ministers like the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Manpower we can move a lot faster toward the day when we call tenders and begin to harness Fundy tidal power. When I watch those tides coming in and going out, reaching a height of 54 feet on occasions, it does not seem realistic to me that all this latent power should not be used to the advantage of this country especially since the engineering expertise is available to us whenever it is required.
In Nova Scotia we are at a particular disadvantage since we are committed to the most expensive energy-producing fuel which exists today, namely, oil. At the same time there is coal galore in our province. When it took office, the Regan government in Nova Scotia embarked on a policy of closing every coal mine which could possibly be closed. Today, it is thinking about opening coal mines. What a sad state of affairs! It may well be that the coal which would be used to produce power in Nova Scotia would not be any cheaper than the oil which is producing it today, but I must say this: If the power were being produced from coal, at least the billions spent on producing it would be staying in Nova Scotia and not going to Venezuela or some other foreign country.
I hope the federal government will wake up the Regan government and induce it to move into coal and coal mines a lot faster than it is doing now. I am not thinking only of coal mines. We might well take an example from South Africa where, by making use of the gasification process, they not only produce gas but also produce petroleum for use in their automobiles. If it can be done in South Africa, it can be done here provided we have the desire and the determination. That is what we are lacking today. We lack the leadership, the desire and the determination to overcome the adversity which faces some parts of Canada. The government needs to wake up, or else some new people are needed in the government, people with a desire to produce the programs the people want and need. An election and a change of government would do the country an awful lot of good.
Before I conclude I should like to make one comment on external affairs. It relates to the Taiwan affair. I was extremely disappointed over the government's attitude toward that small democratic nation.

speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It is nice to hear some people laugh, but I would suggest to you that democracy lives and thrives in Taiwan while the antithesis of democracy exists on mainland China. There is no freedom there for anyone at any time. I
suggest to hon. members who have not been to Taiwan and have not studied the democratic system which exists there that they should read something about it, and perhaps they would not be so critical.
Ad hon. Member: How many parties do they have?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
They have a lot more than they do on the mainland. They do not have marshalls and palace guards and things of that nature who have no respect for the freedom of the people or their lives, and that is the situation on the mainland where 800 million people are being controlled under the yoke of tyranny and totalitarianism. If that is what this government wants, that is fine, but I want to stick with democratic nations and peoples who are our friends, and have been our friends through war and peace.
The sooner this or another government wakes up to the fact that our best partners are those democratic nations of this world the better off and the happier all Canadians will be. If the government wants to know why its state is so low at this point in time I suggest it is because of situations that have developed in this country since 1974, such as the Taiwan affair, which destroyed and will continue to destroy the credibility of the government.
The final thing I wish to suggest is that we have another oasis of freedom in the Middle East in Israel. I hope the government will continue to assist that small nation in developing in the way it has, and to see that its boundaries are defensible and secure so its people can enjoy freedom of life, peace, and security. I am not critical about the government's policy as far as Israel is concerned, but I would refer to the remarks of the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe regarding the passport situation. This involved people travelling to Arab countries with stamps in their passports indicating they were non-Jews. That is a despicable thing to have happen to anyone in this country. I cannot understand how any government agency would be allowed to put such a policy into effect. Canadians are entitled to an explanation of how that happened, and an assurance that the people involved are no longer associated with external affairs. Canadians would then be a great deal happier about the situation.
My time has just about expired. Before I sit down I should once again like to urge the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Manpower and Immigration to assist in developing some kind of monitoring agency to see that regional programs in Atlantic Canada are made workable and effective in overcoming the regional disparity there. I hope they will make sure that national programs do not thwart the intentions of regional policies.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: UNVEILING OF STATUE OF RIGHT HON. LOUIS ST. LAURENT SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
We are
honouring today the memory of a man who, in spite of staggering odds, served his country exceptionally well.
Nothing seemed to incline the lawyer Louis St. Laurent to politics and even less to mack him out for the highest office in government. Yet, at an age where others are already considering retirement, he acceeded to supreme power and pursued one of the most remarkable political careers in our history.

The unpredictability, the impassioned debate and the frustrations that mark political life could not have been attractive to this man of order and reason, of measured, regular habits. But when he entered the political arena the war was raging and a formidable crisis threatened the country.
It was only out of duty that Louis St. Laurent took the first step which would lead him so far, involve him for so long and demand so much of his energy and himself. It was out of duty that he responded the first time to Mackenzie King's call to succeed Ernest Lapointe as Minister of Justice and leader of French Canada. Later, again out of duty, he accepted the External Affairs portfolio that his leader pressed upon him.
And finally, out of duty once more, he yielded to the wishes of Mackenzie King who saw him as his successor, and he became Prime Minister of Canada.
Thus, each of the major stages in his political career began in the austere and pure light of duty. The same moral purpose guided and directed all his actions, whether dealing with his French-speaking compatriots or the country as a whole.
[ Translation]
He had a deep love for Canada and never questioned the concept of our Canadian identity, which explains his almost religious concern for Canadian unity. In that respect, he did not hesitate to jeopardize his prestige, his popularity and his political capital. And the people whom he trusted, proved him right. His courage and his devotion to duty were a lesson and a salvation for the whole country. Such broad and rigorous views guided his actions on the international level. His name remains linked to some achievements which safeguard the western world to this day and contribute to world peace.
A true Canadian, an exemplary citizen, a first-rate politician, Louis St. Laurent won world-wide recognition and acclaim. May this monument which I have the honour to unveil, as well as the square and spacious grounds which will bear his name, perpetuate forever the memory of the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent as well as the example of his remarkable virtues.

October 15, 1976
